title: The corporation as a separate person: limited liability and its limits
summary: A corporation is a separate legal person that owns its own assets and owes its own debts, which is what gives shareholders limited liability. This lesson explains that protection and the common ways owners lose it, from personal guarantees to director liabilities and commingling.
body:
Bottom line. In law, a corporation is a separate person. It owns its assets, signs its contracts and owes its own debts. That is why shareholders usually risk only what they put in. But the protection has known gaps, and most owners lose it by their own signature or their own habits, not by bad luck.

In plain English

Mr Shabazz, when you form a company, you create a new legal person. It is not you, even if you own every share. It can own land, borrow money, hire people, sue and be sued in its own name. This idea is old and settled in common-law countries. The classic case is Salomon v A Salomon and Company Limited, decided by the House of Lords in England in 1897, which confirmed that a properly formed company is a separate person from its owner.

From that idea comes limited liability. If the company cannot pay its debts, the creditors can take the company's assets. As a general rule, they cannot take the shareholders' personal assets. The shareholder's loss is limited to the money invested in the shares.

That is the protection. The rest of this lesson is about its limits, because a developer who assumes the protection is complete can lose it without noticing.

The framework

  1. The company is the party. Contracts, bank accounts and title should be in the company's exact legal name. Under the Canada Business Corporations Act, section 15, a corporation has the capacity and the rights, powers and privileges of a natural person. Provincial statutes such as Alberta's have similar provisions.
  2. Personal guarantees. The most common gap. A guarantee is your personal promise to pay the company's debt if it does not. Lenders, landlords and suppliers often require one. Once you sign, limited liability does not protect you for that debt.
  3. Your own wrongs. If you personally act negligently or dishonestly, for example by making a false statement to a buyer, you may be personally liable for what you did, even while acting for the company.
  4. Director liabilities set by statute. Some laws make directors personally liable for certain company debts. Examples are unpaid employee wages, under section 119 of the Canada Business Corporations Act, and unremitted payroll deductions, under section 227.1 of the Income Tax Act (Canada). These usually come with defences for directors who acted with due diligence.
  5. Piercing the corporate veil. In rare cases, courts disregard the separate person, usually where the company was used as a sham or to commit fraud. This is exceptional, but careless habits make the argument easier.
  6. Commingling. Mixing company money with personal money, or one company's money with another's, weakens the separation in practice and in any later dispute.

A worked example

Hypothetical. A developer owns all the shares of a company that buys a lot for 1,000,000, funded with 200,000 of the developer's equity and an 800,000 loan. The lender requires the developer's personal guarantee.

Two years later, the project stalls and the land is sold by the lender for 650,000. The company still owes 150,000 plus costs. Without the guarantee, the developer's loss would usually be the 200,000 invested, and the lender's remaining claim would be against the company only. With the guarantee, the lender can pursue the developer personally for the 150,000 shortfall.

Now add a habit. During those two years the developer paid some personal bills from the company account and some company bills from a personal card. In a dispute, that mixing makes it harder to show where the company ended and the owner began.

Better protection would have been a guarantee capped at a fixed amount, ending when a set loan-to-value is reached, and clean, separate accounts throughout.

Professional Sign-Off Required: independent legal counsel for the guarantor before any guarantee is signed.

The beginner mistake

Believing that "putting it in a company" protects you, and then signing a personal guarantee for every major debt. At that point, for those debts, the company is mostly a label. A second mistake is treating the company's bank account as your own. Separation is a legal fact, but it is also a habit, and courts look at habits.

How you will use it

Keep a register of every personal guarantee you have signed: the creditor, the amount, any cap and the end date. Review it every year and ask lenders to release guarantees once the project is stable.

Before you sign any contract, check that the party is the company, under its exact legal name, and that you sign with your title, for example "per: name, President". Signing without the title can blur whether you signed for the company or for yourself.

And keep every company's money in its own accounts, with every movement between them documented. Topic 5 covers this in detail.

Finally, remember the director liabilities. If you are a director, ask your bookkeeper every month to confirm that payroll deductions, sales taxes and wages are paid on time. These are the debts most likely to follow a director home, and a monthly confirmation is also evidence of the care the law expects.
checklist: Sign every contract in the company's exact legal name, with your title.
Keep a register of every personal guarantee you have signed.
Negotiate a cap and an end date on every guarantee.
Know the director liabilities for wages and payroll remittances.
Keep company money and personal money in separate accounts.
Document every movement of money between you and the company.

selftest.q: Your company is about to sign a five-year lease. The landlord asks you to sign the lease "personally and on behalf of the company". What has changed, and what could you negotiate?
selftest.a: Signing personally makes you a party to the lease or a guarantor of it, so for that obligation you no longer have limited liability. Over five years the exposure could be all the remaining rent. Negotiate to sign only for the company, with your title. If the landlord insists on personal support, offer a separate guarantee that is capped at a fixed amount, such as a number of months of rent, and that ends after a set period of on-time payment. Professional Sign-Off Required: commercial leasing counsel.

apply: List every personal guarantee you have signed. For each, write the creditor, the maximum amount, any cap and any end date. Mark any you cannot find the terms for, and request copies.
sources: Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd [1897] AC 22 (House of Lords). Canada Business Corporations Act, RSC 1985, c C-44, sections 15 and 119. Income Tax Act (Canada), RSC 1985, c 1 (5th Supp), section 227.1. Statute sections are cited from the author's working knowledge of the federal Act and should be read on the official Justice Laws website before being relied on; the Alberta Business Corporations Act, RSA 2000, c B-9, has broadly similar concepts but different section numbers [Alberta section numbers unverified — confirm independently]. Veil piercing is described as a general concept only. All figures are hypothetical. Education only.

title: Shares, classes and rights: voting, dividends, redemption
summary: A share is a bundle of rights, and a company can create different classes of shares with different bundles. Knowing the three core rights, voting, dividends and a share of what is left at the end, and how classes split them, lets you design ownership deliberately.
body:
Bottom line. A share is not a slice of the company. It is a bundle of rights set out in the company's articles. The core rights are to vote, to receive dividends when declared, and to share in what is left when the company is wound up. Different classes of shares split those rights in different ways, and the split decides who controls the company and who gets paid.

In plain English

Mr Shabazz, most people picture shares as equal pieces of a cake. In law, a share is closer to a ticket with rules printed on the back. The rules are written in the articles of incorporation, which is the company's founding document filed with the government registry.

The rules answer three questions. Can this share vote? Can this share receive dividends, and in what order? What does this share receive if the company is wound up and its assets are distributed?

A company can have several classes of shares, each with its own answers. One class may vote but receive dividends last. Another may not vote but be paid first. That flexibility is why share structure is one of the main tools for control, for bringing in investors, and for tax planning.

The framework

  1. Voting. Voting shares elect the directors and approve major changes. Whoever controls the votes controls the board, and the board runs the company.
  2. Dividends. A dividend is a payment of profit to shareholders, declared by the directors. Shares can have dividends that are discretionary, meaning the directors choose whether to pay that class, or preferred, meaning that class is paid a set amount before others. Preferred dividends can be cumulative, meaning unpaid amounts carry forward, or non-cumulative.
  3. Liquidation rights. When the company is wound up, debts are paid first. What remains goes to shareholders in the order the articles set. Preferred shares often get their fixed amount back before common shares share the rest.
  4. Redemption and retraction. A redemption right lets the company buy back the shares at a set price. A retraction right lets the shareholder require the company to buy them back. These are common in estate freezes and investor deals. Payments are usually subject to solvency tests in the corporate statute.
  5. Common and preferred. Common shares usually carry the residual value: the growth after everyone ahead of them is paid. Preferred shares usually carry a fixed value and priority.
  6. Tax rules travel with dividends. Paying dividends to family members through share classes is limited by tax rules, including the tax on split income in section 120.4 of the Income Tax Act (Canada). Share design for family members always needs tax advice.

A worked example

Hypothetical. A developer's company has three classes.

ClassVotesDividendsOn wind-up
Class A commonYesDiscretionaryShare of what is left
Class B commonNoDiscretionaryShare of what is left
Class C preferredNoUp to 5 percent a year, non-cumulativePaid 500,000 first, redeemable at 500,000

The developer holds all 100 Class A shares, so controls the board. An investor contributes 500,000 for the Class C shares. Ten years later the company is wound up with 2,000,000 left after debts. The Class C holder receives 500,000 first. The remaining 1,500,000 is shared among the common shares, Class A and Class B, according to their numbers.

If the investor had instead taken common shares, the investor would have shared in the growth, but would have had no priority if things went badly. The class chosen decides the risk and the reward.

Professional Sign-Off Required: corporate counsel to draft the share terms, and a tax advisor before any shares are issued to family members.

The beginner mistake

Issuing shares from a standard template without reading what rights they carry, and then discovering years later that the class given to a partner can vote, or that the class meant for growth is behind a preferred class that takes everything in a modest sale. The second mistake is designing share classes to move income to family members without tax advice. The tax rules in this area are strict.

How you will use it

For every company you own, make a one-page share table like the one above: each class, who holds it, how many, and its voting, dividend, wind-up and redemption rights. Read it against the articles, which are the primary source.

Before you bring in any investor, decide what you want them to have: priority, growth, a vote, or a way out. Then choose or create the class that gives exactly that. Before any share issue, check what approvals the articles, the by-laws and any shareholder agreement require, and record the issue in the minute book.

Also check the money side. When a company issues shares, the amount paid is added to the stated capital of that class, which is an accounting and legal figure that matters later for redemptions, dividends and tax. Ask your accountant to confirm the stated capital of each class each year, so that the figure in the books matches the figure in the minute book.
checklist: Read the share rights in the articles, not a summary.
List each class, its holders and numbers.
Note voting, dividend, wind-up and redemption rights for each class.
Decide what an investor should get before choosing a class.
Check required approvals before issuing shares.
Get tax advice before issuing shares to family members.
Record every share issue in the minute book.

selftest.q: A partner offers 300,000 for a 30 percent stake in your company and asks for "common shares, same as yours". What should you think about?
selftest.a: If the partner receives the same class as you, they get the same vote per share, so 30 percent of the votes, and a full share of the growth. Ask what you want them to have. If you want to keep control, consider a non-voting common class, or keep voting control through numbers. If they want protection, they may ask for preferred terms instead. Also check whether existing shareholders have a right to buy new shares first, what approvals are needed, and whether a shareholder agreement should govern transfers and exits. Professional Sign-Off Required: corporate counsel and a tax advisor.

apply: Find the articles for one of your companies. Build a one-page table of each share class: votes, dividends, wind-up rights, redemption or retraction, and who holds it today.
sources: Share rights are set by each company's articles under its governing corporate statute; this lesson describes common patterns, not any company's actual terms. Income Tax Act (Canada), section 120.4 (tax on split income), named as a concept only; its application is complex and must be confirmed with a tax advisor. Statute sections are cited from the author's working knowledge of the federal Act and should be read on the official Justice Laws website before being relied on; the Alberta Business Corporations Act, RSA 2000, c B-9, has broadly similar concepts but different section numbers [Alberta section numbers unverified — confirm independently]. All figures are hypothetical. Education only.

title: Directors, officers, shareholders: duties and the minute book
summary: Shareholders own, directors manage and officers carry out, and each role has its own powers and duties. The minute book is the written proof of who decided what, and keeping it current is one of the cheapest protections a company has.
body:
Bottom line. A company has three roles. Shareholders own it and elect the directors. Directors manage it and owe it legal duties. Officers run it day to day. Even when one person holds all three roles, the law treats them as separate, and the minute book is where you prove each decision was made by the right person in the right way.

In plain English

Mr Shabazz, in a small company it is common for one person to be the only shareholder, the only director and the president. It feels like one job. In law it is three jobs, and each has different powers.

Shareholders vote on a short list of big things: electing directors, approving fundamental changes such as amending the articles or selling substantially all of the company's assets. Directors make the major decisions in between: borrowing, issuing shares, declaring dividends, appointing officers. Officers, such as a president or secretary, carry out the directors' decisions and manage the business.

The minute book is the company's official record. It holds the articles, the by-laws, the registers of shareholders and directors, and the minutes and resolutions that record decisions. When a bank, a buyer or a court asks "who approved this?", the minute book is the answer.

The framework

  1. The duty of loyalty. Directors and officers must act honestly and in good faith with a view to the best interests of the corporation. This is in section 122 of the Canada Business Corporations Act. The Supreme Court of Canada discussed this duty in Peoples Department Stores v Wise, 2004, and BCE Inc v 1976 Debentureholders, 2008, explaining that the duty is owed to the corporation, and that directors may consider the interests of shareholders, creditors and others.
  2. The duty of care. The same section requires the care, diligence and skill that a reasonably prudent person would show in comparable circumstances. In practice: be informed, ask questions, rely on proper advice, and record that you did.
  3. Conflicts of interest. A director who has an interest in a contract with the company must disclose it and, in general, not vote on it. The federal rule is in section 120 of the Canada Business Corporations Act.
  4. Meetings and written resolutions. Decisions are made at meetings or by written resolution signed by all directors or all voting shareholders entitled to vote. In small companies, signed written resolutions are the usual method.
  5. The annual cycle. Each year: approve the financial statements, elect or confirm directors, appoint or waive an auditor where allowed, and file the annual return with the registry.
  6. The registers. Keep current registers of shareholders, directors, and in many places individuals with significant control. Update them on every change.

A worked example

Hypothetical. A developer is the sole director of a company. The company lends 150,000 to another company the developer owns. Nobody records anything.

Three years later the first company applies for a construction loan. The lender's lawyer reviews the minute book and finds no resolution approving the loan, no loan agreement, no disclosure of the developer's interest in the borrower, and no annual resolutions for two years. The lender delays funding until the records are corrected. The fix costs legal fees and, more importantly, weeks.

The clean version would have taken an hour at the time: a director's resolution approving the loan on stated terms, a note recording the developer's interest in the borrower, a signed loan agreement, and the annual resolutions signed each year.

Professional Sign-Off Required: corporate counsel to review and correct the minute book.

The beginner mistake

Running the company as if you were the company. Decisions are made in conversation and never recorded. When the company is later sold, financed or audited, the missing records cost far more to rebuild than they would have cost to keep. The second mistake is forgetting that duties are owed to the company, not to you as owner, which matters when creditors are not paid.

How you will use it

Treat the minute book as a working file, not a box in a lawyer's office. After every significant decision, such as a loan, a share issue, a large contract, a dividend or a change of officers, ask: who has the power to make this decision, and has it been recorded?

Set an annual reminder for each company to sign the annual resolutions and file the annual return. Keep a scanned copy of the minute book where you can find it. Lenders and buyers will ask for it, and a complete, current book makes you look like what you are: a careful operator.

One more habit protects you as a director. When the company makes a large or risky decision, record the information the directors relied on: the appraisal, the lender's term sheet, the professional advice. If the decision is ever questioned, that record is evidence that you met the duty of care. A decision that turned out badly is not a breach of duty if it was informed, honest and made in good faith.
checklist: Know which role, shareholder, director or officer, makes each decision.
Record every significant decision by minutes or signed resolution.
Disclose any personal interest in a company contract and record it.
Sign annual resolutions and file the annual return each year.
Keep the share, director and significant-control registers current.
Keep a scanned copy of the minute book you can produce quickly.

selftest.q: You are the only director of your company. You want the company to pay your other company 20,000 a month in management fees. What should be in the minute book?
selftest.a: A disclosure that you have an interest in the other company, recorded in the minutes or resolution. A director's resolution approving the management agreement and its terms, with a note of why it is in the company's best interests. A signed written management agreement setting the services, the fee and how it can be ended. Evidence that the fee reflects real services at a fair rate. Because you are the only director, the disclosure and the business reason are especially important, and tax rules on related-party fees also apply. Professional Sign-Off Required: corporate counsel and a tax advisor.

apply: Open the minute book of one of your companies. Check that it has the articles, the by-laws, current registers, and signed annual resolutions for each of the last three years. List what is missing and send the list to your lawyer.
sources: Canada Business Corporations Act, RSC 1985, c C-44, sections 120 and 122. Peoples Department Stores Inc (Trustee of) v Wise, 2004 SCC 68. BCE Inc v 1976 Debentureholders, 2008 SCC 69. Statute sections are cited from the author's working knowledge of the federal Act and should be read on the official Justice Laws website before being relied on; the Alberta Business Corporations Act, RSA 2000, c B-9, has broadly similar concepts but different section numbers [Alberta section numbers unverified — confirm independently]. Requirements for significant-control registers and annual filings vary by jurisdiction [confirm independently]. All figures are hypothetical. Education only.

title: Shareholder agreements: control, exits, deadlock, death
summary: A shareholder agreement is the contract between owners that decides who controls the company, how someone can leave, what happens when owners disagree, and what happens if one of them dies. Writing it while everyone gets along is far cheaper than fighting about it later.
body:
Bottom line. Corporate law gives a default set of rules. A shareholder agreement replaces the defaults with rules the owners choose: who controls which decisions, how an owner can leave, how a deadlock is broken, and what happens on death or disability. Sign it while everyone agrees. That is the only time it is cheap.

In plain English

Mr Shabazz, when two or more people own a company together, the corporate statute decides most things by majority vote. That works until it does not. A 50-50 company has no majority. A minority owner can be outvoted on everything. An owner who wants to leave may find nobody will buy a minority stake in a private company. And when an owner dies, their shares pass to their estate, which may mean a spouse or child the other owners have never worked with.

A shareholder agreement is a contract among the shareholders, and usually the company, that sets the rules for all of these situations in advance. In federal Canadian law, an agreement signed by all shareholders that restricts the directors' powers is called a unanimous shareholder agreement, under section 146 of the Canada Business Corporations Act, and it has special effects, including moving some director responsibilities to the shareholders. Provincial statutes have similar concepts.

The framework

  1. Control. Who appoints the directors? Which decisions need more than a simple majority? A list of reserved matters, such as borrowing above a set amount, issuing shares, selling land or changing the business, protects minority owners.
  2. Transfers. Restrictions on selling shares. A right of first refusal means an owner who wants to sell to an outsider must first offer the shares to the other owners on the same terms.
  3. Tag-along and drag-along. A tag-along right lets a minority owner join a sale by the majority on the same terms. A drag-along right lets a majority that has found a buyer require the minority to sell too, so the buyer can get the whole company.
  4. Exits and deadlock. A deadlock is when owners with equal power cannot agree. Common tools are escalation to mediation, and a buy-sell clause, sometimes called a shotgun clause, in which one owner names a price and the other must either buy at that price or sell at that price.
  5. Death and disability. The agreement can require the company or the surviving owners to buy the shares of an owner who dies or becomes disabled, often funded by life insurance, at a price set by a formula or valuation.
  6. Valuation. State how shares are valued for every forced sale: a formula, an independent valuator, or an agreed figure updated every year.
  7. Disputes and new owners. Say how disputes are resolved, and require every new shareholder to sign the agreement.

A worked example

Hypothetical. Two developers each own 50 percent of a company that holds a property worth 2,000,000 after debt. They disagree about whether to sell. Neither has a majority, so the company cannot act.

Their agreement has a shotgun clause. One developer offers to buy the other's half for 1,000,000. The other must either accept 1,000,000 and leave, or buy the first developer's half for 1,000,000. Because the person naming the price might end up on either side of it, there is pressure to name a fair figure.

The clause has a weakness: it favours the owner who has cash or financing ready. If one developer cannot raise 1,000,000 quickly, they may be forced to sell at a price they consider too low. A well-drafted agreement gives a reasonable period to arrange financing.

The same agreement also says that if an owner dies, the company buys the shares at the last agreed annual value, funded by a 1,000,000 life insurance policy on each owner. That keeps the surviving owner in control and gives the family cash instead of a minority stake.

Professional Sign-Off Required: corporate counsel for the agreement, a tax advisor for the insurance and buyout structure, and an insurance professional for the policies.

The beginner mistake

Not signing one, because the owners trust each other. Trust is exactly why it is easy to agree now. The second mistake is signing one and never updating the agreed value, so a death buyout years later happens at a price that bears no relation to the real value.

How you will use it

Before you take on any co-owner or investor, settle five things in writing: control and reserved matters, transfer restrictions, how someone leaves, how deadlock is broken, and what happens on death or disability. Then set a yearly reminder to update the agreed share value and check that insurance still matches it.

If you already have co-owners and no agreement, raise it now, while the business is calm. Disagreement is not the time to write the rules.

Read the agreement with your estate plan beside it. Your will, your powers of attorney and your shareholder agreement must point in the same direction. If your will leaves your shares to your children but the agreement requires the company to buy them, the agreement will usually control what actually happens, so your family should know that in advance.
checklist: Agree who appoints directors and which decisions are reserved.
Include transfer restrictions and a right of first refusal.
Decide on tag-along and drag-along rights.
Choose a deadlock tool and allow time to finance a buyout.
Plan the buyout on death or disability, and how it is funded.
Set the valuation method and update the agreed value yearly.
Require every new shareholder to sign the agreement.

selftest.q: You and a partner each own 50 percent of a company. You have no shareholder agreement. Your partner dies, and their shares pass to their adult child, who wants to sell the company's main property immediately. What is your position?
selftest.a: Weak. Without an agreement, the child, through the estate, now holds 50 percent and the company is deadlocked: you cannot outvote them and they cannot outvote you. You have no right to buy their shares, no agreed price, and no insurance to fund a buyout. The likely paths are negotiation, a court application, or a sale nobody planned. This is exactly the situation a shareholder agreement with a funded death buyout prevents. Professional Sign-Off Required: corporate counsel and an estate lawyer.

apply: List every company you co-own. Next to each, write whether a shareholder agreement exists, when it was last updated, and whether it covers deadlock and death. Book a review for any that is missing or more than three years old.
sources: Canada Business Corporations Act, RSC 1985, c C-44, section 146 (unanimous shareholder agreements). Statute sections are cited from the author's working knowledge of the federal Act and should be read on the official Justice Laws website before being relied on; the Alberta Business Corporations Act, RSA 2000, c B-9, has broadly similar concepts but different section numbers [Alberta section numbers unverified — confirm independently]. Shotgun, tag-along, drag-along and right-of-first-refusal clauses are contract terms, not statutory rules; their enforceability depends on drafting. All figures are hypothetical. Education only.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: corporate counsel for the agreement, a tax advisor for the insurance and buyout structure, and an insurance professional for the policies.
